shax 0.1

Product description

Shax (also known as Jar) is an abstract strategy game with custodian capture rules, played on a 5X5 board. The game consists of two phases: a placement phase followed by a movement and capture phase. Shax is popular in East Africa, and while its exact origin is unknown, it is closely related to Seega, a traditional game from Egypt.

This demo showcases an AI engine for Shax, implemented using Monte Carlos tree search algorithm. Rather than solving the game exhaustively, the engine optimally traverses through the nodes to identify strong moves. The demo also includes visualization of the moves explored by MCTS with metadata attached to individual nodes.

Move Logic Pipeline


MCTS

Game decisions form a branching search space, too large to fully calculate. A greedy policy takes the immediate best reward but often fails long term. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) tackles this by running simulated rollouts and updating value estimates at each branch. Its key innovation is balancing exploration and exploitation, much like modern AI agents do when learning from experience. Over many iterations, the search converges toward optimal strategies without needing prior training data.

In small games like tic-tac-toe, the state space is tiny enough that the full game tree can be pre-computed. But in larger games that scale toward PSPACE-hard or even EXPTIME-level complexity, the branching and depth explode, making exhaustive search impossible. This is where Monte Carlo Tree Search proves valuable: by running targeted simulations, it can handle decision spaces far beyond what brute-force methods allow.

Heuristic Board analysis

Relying only on capture value for scoring node is inefficient generally and outright fail in the first phase since it’s the placement phase. therefore it’s necessary to analyze the board and give heuristic value.

Currently there are 5 pattern we use, if they’re found in the board an extra value is give to the board. if the player is actively threatening a piece they also get point. if the player puts piece in negative positions they lose a point -negative positions marked Red X are position which block advantageous movement and most pattern have negative position-

The five patterns are as follow:

Knight control (+2pts), Rook control (+2pts), Solo corner control (+1pt), Duo corner control, Trio edge control (+2pts).

Every instance of the game board can be analyzed and given a score. for example this board below has score of xyx from blue side.

Miscellaneous

[my version]

There were numerous problems faced in making the engine. Initially there was no simulation in the MCTS this caused the moves to be uninspiring and predictable while also reducing entropy. there was also the cases of AI becoming too defensive and other cases of it becoming careless about the danger; this hubris was due to the lack of Bi-turn backpropagation. And finally the hardest problem to solve OOM-out of memory-. In this section, will go through them in details.

During the early development of the engine, the AI was too defensive because all backpropagation stages were values the same, this was fixed by adding exponential decay along the backpropagation. and in the case were the AI was too offensive, this was triggered because half the nodes are disproportionate [ends without complete bi-turn cycles]. For example, if the AI count odd moves like ‘AI->human->AI’ it would assume it has advantage when in reality it should’ve considered the following opponents move. this was a particularly hindering problem and it’s solution is to stop backpropagation only at even moves.

OOM or ‘out of memory exception’ was particularly re-occurring problem in the web build of the engine. this was due to the reality that AI algorithm require a huge memory. My jar-engine suffered from 1.5 GB of memory spike after every calculation. this was because every node was this was because i had a heuristic function with 10 list<int[2]>, each list containing 4 int[2]; the heuristic function is called 5 times per node and there are 30,000 node. this calls for 6 million heap allocation causing ludicrous memory spike. the solution was to switch from list to struct to avoid constant allocation followed de-allocation in the heap. and any list which couldn’t be changed to struct were kept with the use scratchpad which is basically reusing the same list by manually clearing it with each use. these 2 solutions made the spike to a 100 MB per MCTS calculation reducing 75% from the original spike.

[gpt version]

Several challenges arose during the development of the engine. Initially, the absence of simulation in the MCTS resulted in moves that were predictable and uninspiring, with reduced entropy. In some cases, the AI became overly defensive, while in others it neglected potential dangers; this inconsistency stemmed from the lack of bi-turn backpropagation. The most difficult issue, however, was out-of-memory (OOM) errors. In this section, each of these problems will be discussed in detail.

During the early stages of development, the AI often played too defensively because all stages of backpropagation were weighted equally. This issue was resolved by applying exponential decay along the backpropagation path. Conversely, when the AI played too aggressively, the problem stemmed from nodes that ended prematurely, without completing a full bi-turn cycle. For example, after a sequence like AI → Human → AI, the engine mistakenly assumed an advantage, without accounting for the opponent’s next move. This significantly hindered performance. The solution was to restrict backpropagation to even-numbered moves, ensuring that evaluations always reflected complete cycles.

Out-of-memory (OOM) exceptions were a recurring problem in the web build of the engine, primarily because AI algorithms demand substantial memory. The jar-engine in particular experienced spikes of up to 1.5 GB after each calculation. This occurred because the heuristic function used ten List<int[2]>, each containing four int[2]. Since the heuristic was invoked five times per node across 30,000 nodes, the process required approximately six million heap allocations, leading to severe memory overhead.

To address this, two optimizations were introduced. First, lists were replaced with structs wherever possible to avoid repeated allocation and deallocation on the heap. Second, for lists that could not be converted, a “scratchpad” approach was adopted—reusing the same list by manually clearing it between uses. These changes reduced the memory spike to about 100 MB per MCTS calculation, a 75% improvement compared to the original implementation.
